title: Foundations: how these systems work
intro: Everything in this course rests on a handful of mechanisms: what a language model actually does when it answers, what it can and cannot remember, and why a fluent answer is not the same thing as a true one. This chapter builds that foundation from zero. Read it with an assistant open - several sections end with a prompt to run, copied from a named tab of Course_Workbook.xlsx in the deliverables folder.

sections.heading: One skill, two ways to work

blocks.text: Prompting is the one AI skill that transfers everywhere: every assistant, every vendor, every year. Models change monthly; the craft compounds. The skill has two modes. In ASK mode you request an answer or a draft, read it, check it, and decide what happens next. In DELEGATE mode you assign bounded work: you specify the inputs, checks, permissions, and finished result, and the system plans, uses tools, checks itself, and delivers.

The ten-second version: a generative prompt describes what to write; an agentic prompt describes a job to run. That distinction is the backbone of this course - the craft chapters teach the first kind, the agentic chapters grow it into the second. For now, feel the difference.

blocks.text: Step one is ASK: instant text, every unknown guessed. Step two is the seed of DELEGATE: the questions come to you. If your assistant asks questions in step one too, that is no failure - asking is the delegate move; step two makes it happen on purpose.

sections.heading: Four eras, and the decade of named leaps

blocks.text: Seventy years of AI compress into four eras. In the rules era (1950s-1990s), humans hand-coded the logic: if X, then Y. Expert systems did real work - MYCIN diagnosed infections, XCON configured computers - but rules crack on messy reality, and hype outran results twice, in the funding collapses remembered as the AI winters: skepticism is historically earned. In the learning era (1990s-2010s) the approach inverted: let the system find patterns in examples. It gave us spam filters, search ranking, recommendations, and - decisively in 2012, when deep networks on gaming GPUs cut image-recognition error from 26.2% to 15.3% (AlexNet) - modern image recognition.

The generative era began in 2017 with the Transformer, which lets models learn patterns from large datasets: predict-the-next-word at that scale writes, summarizes, and codes, and ChatGPT (2022) made it something everyone could talk to. The agentic era (2024 onward) gives models arms - tools, browsers, files, code - and reasoning models that plan multi-step work and execute it with limited supervision. AI you delegate to.

blocks.title: Why the last decade exploded
blocks.body: Scaling laws (2020): a bigger model, more data, and more compute produced improved measured performance under the studied conditions. Progress stopped being a research gamble and became an investment roadmap.

rows: The Transformer (Attention Is All You Need)
A foundation for many subsequent language models
Show examples in the prompt and it does the task - prompt engineering is born
Human feedback turns a predictor into an assistant; ChatGPT reaches 100M users in two months
Compute spent at answer time, not just in training
Frontier ability gets radically cheaper; big models teach small ones
blocks.note: Each method on this list returns later in the course - treat it as vocabulary.

blocks.text: Adoption outran precedent: ChatGPT reached 100 million users in about two months - the fastest consumer ramp on record at the time (UBS/Reuters, 2023), against roughly nine for TikTok and thirty for Instagram. Access changed faster than workplace processes adapted; that gap is why this course exists.
The hardware, in scoped terms

Two principles are enough. Training: large models learn from repeated computation over data, so parallel processors, memory, and data movement constrain what can be trained. Serving: each request also requires computation, so model design, requested reasoning effort, and workload drive response time and operating cost. Reading hardware claims, keep three categories separate: measured results, estimates, and announced investments.

sections.heading: How a language model produces an answer

blocks.text: The useful mental model: a prediction engine, sent to finishing school. In pretraining, the model spends months on trillions of words learning one task - predict the next token - and language, facts, and reasoning patterns compress into billions of learned weights. Instruction tuning uses curated example dialogues to teach it to follow instructions rather than merely continue your text. Human feedback (RLHF) then tunes it toward helpful, honest, and harmless, from people ranking outputs. How your own feedback and chats are used depends on the product, account, and data settings - check, don't assume.

Two consequences follow. First, knowledge is frozen at the training cutoff, months before release - which is why assistants bolt on escape hatches: live web search pulls today's pages into the prompt, and retrieval plugs in your own documents (below). Second, the model completes your text. The prompt is one way to steer the work, alongside sources, tools, and settings - and a complete prompt does not make the model smarter. It deletes wrong guesses.

blocks.title: Prediction, not verification
blocks.body: A language model predicts useful continuations; it does not independently verify truth. A fluent answer can still contain an unsupported claim.

blocks.text:
SEND 1: Finish this sentence 5 different ways: We should move the launch date because
SEND 2: Now 5 more ways, knowing: B2B software firm, competitor launches May 3, our beta ends April 20.
blocks.caption: Tab EX2-Guesses - two separate sends, in your course log.

blocks.text: The first send scatters across plausible guesses - budget, staffing, quality. The second orbits May 3 and April 20. Grade the directions, not the sentences: your facts deleted wrong guesses. That is your contribution to every answer: the task, the source material, the definitions, and a way to check the result. Compare 'Explain the delay' with 'Explain the delay using these three dated messages' - only the second can be checked. A model filling unstated requirements with its most plausible guess matches what the requester meant only about 41% of the time (Yang, 2026); this course is about closing that gap on purpose.

sections.heading: Tokens and practical limits

blocks.text: The model never sees letters. Text is chopped into tokens - word chunks from a fixed vocabulary, like bricks of text. Common words are one pre-molded brick; rare words get built from pieces (ham-bur-ger). English rules of thumb: one token is about four characters, or three-quarters of a word; a 50-page document runs roughly 25-35 thousand tokens. A token is not a fixed number of words, and limits vary by model and application - check your workspace's actual limits.

Three practical consequences. Everything is priced and limited in tokens - and output typically costs around five times input, because generation is serial - so paste-heavy prompts burn budget and context fast. Non-English and dense technical text cost more tokens for the same meaning. And character-level precision is not the model's native ability: use AI for language and software for characters - counts, checksums, exact IDs.

blocks.title: The strawberry test
blocks.body: The famous letter-counting failures of 2024 (miscounting the r's in 'strawberry') are patched on current frontier models as of September 2026. Still breaking: exact word counts and counting their own tokens on every tier; character-precise edits on fast tiers. For exact checks, count with a tool, not the model.

blocks.text: Explain AI tokens to a high-school student in under 80 words: use a LEGO-brick analogy, show one word splitting into tokens, and end with why tokens set my AI's cost and limits.
blocks.caption: Tab EX3-Tokens - the definition lands in your course log, from your own tool.

sections.heading: Context, saved history, and memory

blocks.text: Three things sound alike and are not. Active context is the information available to the model for this response. Saved chat history is a stored conversation you may be able to reopen - closing a window does not necessarily delete it. Cross-chat memory is a product feature that may carry selected information into other conversations. Only the first is guaranteed to influence the answer in front of you.

For active context, use the desk analogy: the context window is working memory for one conversation. Your question, the system prompt, every prior turn, attached files, and tool results must all fit on the desk. By 2026, roughly one million tokens (about 750,000 words) is the flagship standard - but consumer apps often enforce smaller limits, and a model's published limit may differ from what your interface makes available.

blocks.title: Lost in the middle
blocks.body: In long contexts, accuracy is highest at the start and end and sags in the middle (Liu et al., 2023). Placement alone is worth up to ~30% on long documents (Anthropic's long-context guidance).

items: Long documents at the top, the question at the end - check the effect on your own task.
Label multiple documents so the model can tell them apart.
New topic, new chat - old turns are still on the desk, steering.
Long thread? Run the handoff move below.

blocks.text: Just as important is what the model does not remember. Nothing persists into a fresh conversation unless a memory feature or a saved file reloads it, and a very long chat may compress or omit earlier material. Carry important requirements forward yourself: for a handoff, save the goal, sources, decisions, open items, and next step.

STEP 1: Explain your context window like I'm a 5th grader: the desk, what fits on it, and what happens when I close this chat. Under 100 words.
STEP 2: Summarize our chat so far in under 80 words, titled HANDOFF.
blocks.caption: Tab EX4-Handoff - later, paste the HANDOFF into a fresh chat and ask 'where was I?'

blocks.text: One term to file for the agentic chapters: context engineering. The prompt is the briefing; context is everything on the desk, including things nobody typed - tool results, standing instructions. Agentic tools bolt a filing cabinet onto the desk: persistent files and notes that outlive one conversation.

sections.heading: Answers grounded in documents

blocks.text: The model's built-in knowledge is frozen and public; your work runs on private documents it has never seen. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) bridges that gap at answer time - an open-book exam. You ask a plain question ('What does the supplier agreement say about re-inspection?'); a retrieval step finds the most relevant passages - semantic search, by meaning rather than keywords; those passages land on the model's desk behind the scenes; and the model answers from the supplied text, citing where it looked.

Grounding beats recall for three reasons. It is current: documents are re-indexed in minutes, with no retraining. It is checkable: citations point to the exact passage, which free recall can never do. And it can respect boundaries - though privacy and access depend on the actual service, its permissions, retention, and training-use settings, so confirm what your organization runs. Retrieval feeding one answer is not training the model on your documents; that is the privacy point worth repeating. Many internal document assistants work exactly this way.

blocks.title: The wrong page, beautifully cited
blocks.body: Fetch the wrong page - an outdated revision, a near-miss document - and the model still writes a fluent, confident, cited answer from it. An outdated agreement can support a well-cited but wrong answer for today's decision.

blocks.title: Audit the librarian
blocks.body: Ask for the document, the revision, and the supporting passage. Then read the cited passage and confirm it actually answers the question. Check the citation, not just the prose.

sections.heading: Effort, capability, and the smallest fix

blocks.text: Instructions, sources, and model adaptation

When an answer disappoints, there are three sizes of intervention, and the smallest that solves the problem wins. Clearer instructions fix behavior - tone, format, focus, approach. Better source material fixes missing knowledge - your policies, your data, current facts; most real workplace cases end here. Model adaptation (retraining) changes deep habits permanently; it is slow, expensive, and rare - an IT project, justified only by a recurring need that evaluation shows simpler changes cannot meet. One question picks the level: is the model missing knowledge (supply documents), or misbehaving with knowledge it has (fix the prompt)? More documents or more training do not automatically solve unclear requirements.
Reasoning effort and the task

Assistants ship a fast path - one pass, instant, cheap - and a thinking path that drafts, checks, and revises internally before answering. The model is not literally thinking; it generates intermediate tokens that improve the final answer, and those are billed like output, the expensive kind - a hard question can quietly cost 5-20 times a simple one. Try more effort for a difficult comparison, several dependent calculations, or a result requiring multiple checks; keep it off for lookups, reformatting, summaries, routine drafting. Measure correctness, useful evidence, response time, and cost in the account you actually use, and escalate on failure, not by default - more computation does not replace clear requirements or verification.
Capabilities to look for in an assistant

items: Quick response - when the task is clear and the output is easy to check.
Additional reasoning - for a difficult comparison or a task requiring several checks.
Search or document retrieval - when the answer needs current or supplied source material.
File creation and tool use - when the deliverable includes calculations, editable files, or actions.

blocks.text: Product menus change, and names, limits, and costs vary by vendor and account - so verify current documentation and your account's actual access rather than memorizing a catalog, and never rely on a model's description of where its own buttons live. The durable habit: pick the smallest mode that can succeed, and escalate deliberately.
List the modes this app gives me - quick answer, thinking, web search, deep research, agent - one line each on what it does differently and its rough effort. Say 'unsure' rather than guess.
blocks.caption: Tab EX6-FeatureMenu - self-updating: ask again the day a button changes.

sections.heading: Verification belongs in the task

blocks.text: Now the mechanism that makes verification non-optional. Models are optimized for the most plausible next token, not the most true one, and trouble concentrates where training data is thin: rare facts, citations, numbers, names. OpenAI's own 2025 research adds the incentive: benchmarks reward confident guessing over 'I don't know', so models learn to be good test-takers. The better word than hallucination is confabulation - gaps filled with plausible material, in format: fake citations look exactly like citations.

The effect is measurable. In the comparison OpenAI published in 2025, an older reasoning model answered 24% of hard factual questions right and 75% wrong; a newer model, trained to say 'I don't know', answered 22% right and 26% wrong, abstaining 52% of the time - roughly three times fewer false claims at nearly the same amount right. The confident guess is a training artifact; explicit permission to not know - the move the craft chapters call the Out - recovers the honesty the benchmarks trained away.

blocks.title: 'Are you sure?' is not verification
blocks.body: Pushback is a social signal, not a re-derivation: the model re-reads you, not its work. Answers flip in 58% of cases, 14.7% from right to wrong (SycEval, AIES 2025). Verification is a named check or an outside source - never the same model reassuring you.

blocks.text: So verification belongs in the task itself. 'The supplier approved the change' invites one question: what message supports that claim? 'Approval is conditional on the cost cap' - with the message shown and the condition preserved - can be checked, and keeps the qualifier that makes it true. When you set a task, name the source or calculation that would settle the question.

blocks.title: The rule of three
blocks.body: For numbers, recompute. For claims, inspect the source. For actions, inspect the result.

blocks.text: The public record shows what skipping the check costs. In June 2023 a New York lawyer filed six cases that did not exist - then asked ChatGPT whether they were real, and it said yes ($5,000 sanction, Mata v. Avianca): he checked the fabrication with the fabricator. In February 2024 a tribunal made Air Canada honor a refund policy its website chatbot had invented - your organization owns what its chatbot says. In May 2024 an AI search feature served a joke forum comment as advice: glue in pizza sauce. Across 2025-26, three global consultancies had reports challenged over invented or failed citations, and a legal tracker counted about 1,500 court decisions worldwide involving AI-fabricated citations by mid-2026. Each time, the missing thing was a check someone could have run.

The cure has not changed: ground it (give it the source), cite it (demand receipts, plus an 'I don't know' escape hatch), verify it (check what matters before it ships). None of these eliminates confabulation - they convert unverifiable claims into verifiable ones. House rule from here on: every uncited standard clause, date, number, or quote is a draft until verified.

sections.heading: Failure patterns and the check they need

blocks.text: The last foundation is diagnostic. When an answer is wrong, the reflex is to reword the whole prompt and hope. Resist it: output quality swings up to 76 accuracy points from formatting alone (Sclar et al., ICLR 2024), so one failed phrasing is a data point about the prompt, not the capability ceiling. The productive move is to name what kind of wrong you got, because each kind points at the part of the prompt that owns it - the elements the craft chapters build in full. The grid below is the map the course keeps returning to.

rows: The wrong altitude, tone, or posture
An answer to a different (or vaguer) question
Generically right, specifically wrong for us
Right content, unusable shape or length
Not matching the standard in your head
blocks.note: The diagnosis grid - also on page 1 of references/Elements_of_Prompting_Field_Guide.pdf.

blocks.text: Two rows deserve a word now. 'Generically right, specifically wrong' means the model filled your specifics with the internet's average - the Context row. And the two 'missing' rows are the safety valves: the Out is permission to say 'I don't know'; the Stop is the boundary that turns open-ended capability into bounded work. The rest you will recognize the moment they happen to you.

The same discipline applies to any answer you are about to rely on. Four patterns recur, each with its check: an invented fact - find the supporting record, or state that it is unknown; an invented citation - open the actual source and inspect the cited passage; the wrong document or revision - confirm identity, date, and applicability first; a lost condition - compare the conclusion with the original qualifier or approval condition.

blocks.title: Format is not evidence
blocks.body: A credible format, confident tone, or citation marker is not a substitute for checking. A memorable failure story matters only if it changes which checks you run.

blocks.text: That completes the foundations: two ways of working, a prediction engine steered by what you supply, hard limits on memory and attention, grounding that beats recall, effort dialed to the task, and verification designed into the work. Next comes the craft: turning what you already know about writing requirements into testable prompts - practiced on one fictional supplier case that runs through the whole book.

title: Models and tools: choosing where the work happens
intro: Before you invest in the craft of prompting, spend a few minutes on two decisions that sit upstream of every prompt: which assistant does the work, and which workspace is allowed to see the data. The assistant market re-ranks monthly, so this chapter deliberately teaches you a method for choosing rather than a ranking to memorize. The names churn; the habits you leave with do not.

sections.heading: Compare on your task, not on the leaderboard

blocks.text: Public leaderboards answer a question you are not asking: which model scores highest on someone else's benchmark. Your question is narrower and more useful: which assistant, on the account you actually have, does your task well. The course materials date every product characterization as of September 2026 precisely because such claims expire; the comparison method below does not.
When you need to choose an assistant for a piece of work, walk four questions in order:

items: Required output. Can this account produce the text, calculation, file, or action you need?
Source access. Can it use the right documents and show supporting evidence?
Work environment. Does it fit the approved workspace and collaboration process?
Evaluation. Run the same representative task on the candidates and compare correctness, effort, and cost.

blocks.text: The assistants you will meet by name in this course include ChatGPT, Claude, Copilot, Gemini, Perplexity, and Grok; verify current offerings before relying on any characterization of them. What stays true across the churn is that different assistants expose different capabilities and controls, and the same brand behaves differently on different account tiers. That is why the fourth question, a small head-to-head trial on a task that represents your real work, settles more arguments than any review article.

blocks.title: The rule that survives the churn
blocks.body: Tool choice follows the job, the evidence, and the approved data boundary, not habit and not a leaderboard.

blocks.title: Rankings age in months
blocks.body: Any model ranking or product claim without a date is expired on arrival. Treat dated names and rankings as reference context, not a purchasing guide, and re-verify before a decision that matters.

blocks.title: A ten-minute bake-off
blocks.body: Pick one task that represents your real work. Run the identical prompt in two assistants you can access, then compare correctness, effort, and cost. Keep the result with its date.

sections.heading: January 2025: the efficiency moment

blocks.text: One event explains why the advanced capabilities from Part 1, extended thinking and deep research, did not stay luxury-priced. In January 2025, the Chinese lab DeepSeek released R1, and three facts made it a landmark:

items: DeepSeek-R1 was an open-weights reasoning model rivaling OpenAI's o1, with MIT-licensed weights anyone could download.
Nvidia lost $589 billion in market value in one day (January 27), then the largest single-day market loss ever.
The famous "$5.6M training cost" headline described real efficiency but was oversold: that figure was the fuel for the final race, not the cost of the racing team.

blocks.text: The trick has a name: Mixture of Experts

Picture a huge specialist hospital at night. The building holds 671 billion parameters on the books, but for any one question only about 37 billion wake up: the lit windows, the relevant departments. You pay for the specialists consulted, not for the whole building. Distillation, big models teaching small ones, finishes the job. The result on the bill, per million output tokens as of January 2025: OpenAI's o1 cost $60, DeepSeek-R1 cost $2.19, roughly 27x cheaper. A $100 o1 workload cost about $3.60 on R1.

blocks.note: Scores as reported in the R1 paper, January 2025. Matched on math and coding, behind on PhD-level science: not a clean sweep.

blocks.title: The oversold headline
blocks.body: Quoting "$5.6M to train a frontier model" without its scope repeats a distortion: the number covered one final training run, not the hardware and research behind it. Real efficiency gain, wrong denominator.

blocks.title: Why this belongs in your reference layer
blocks.body: Vendor and pricing history is context, not current guidance. Costs measured on different dates and by different methods are not directly interchangeable; always carry the date with the number.

blocks.text: Explain Mixture of Experts like a colleague: a specialist hospital where only the relevant departments wake up per question — and why that made AI dramatically cheaper in 2025. Under 120 words.

sections.heading: The right workspace for the data

blocks.text: Capability is the second question. The first is where the data may go. Data sensitivity decides the tool, and the decision runs through three checks before anything is uploaded:

items: Approved account. Use the service and the account approved for this work.
Allowed material. Confirm what may be uploaded, retained, and shared.
Minimum access. Give the tool only the files and permissions the task requires.

blocks.text: A vendor's home country alone does not describe every customer's storage arrangement. Company data rules depend on the actual account, service, contract, and configuration. Data residency, choosing where your data lives, is typically an enterprise feature: the same vendor can host your company tenant in the EU while its consumer app stores chats in the United States. Same logo, different homes; the account tier decides which one is yours. The one question that settles it is for your IT department: which region and tier does your account run on? Your organization's AI policy answers everything else.

A distinction worth keeping when open-weights models come up: using a vendor's app is eating at their restaurant, where they see your order. A downloaded open-weights model is a cookbook your IT team can cook from at home. The app, not the model, is where the data-handling risk lives.

This is also why every exercise in this course runs on fictional data: the supplier quality scenario with Alpha Components, Bravo Plastics, and Cardinal Metals in the Data tab of Course_Workbook.xlsx. It behaves like real operational data but is safe in any workspace, so you can practice the craft before you ever face the upload question with real records.

blocks.title: The standing rule
blocks.body: Your organization's AI policy and approved-tool list outrank every product named in this part, and they outrank this book. Where they conflict with anything written here, the policy wins.

blocks.title: Judging by the logo
blocks.body: Inferring where your words go from a vendor's headquarters or brand reputation skips the variable that actually matters: the tier and configuration of the account in front of you.

blocks.title: Before any upload
blocks.body: Name the approved account, the allowed material, and the minimum access for this task. If any of the three is uncertain, resolve it through your organization's approved guidance before uploading, not after.

title: Prompt engineering: writing the work specification
intro: This is the craft chapter: how to get what you actually meant. Its central claim, once seen, is hard to unsee: writing a good prompt is writing a good requirement — and you almost certainly write requirements already. The chapter builds the anatomy of a strong prompt, walks the menu of requirement types, and puts both on an improvement loop.

sections.heading: You already write work specifications

blocks.text: Start with a recognition. Requirements, standard operating procedures, and test protocols exercise one core skill: stating what a piece of work must contain, how it must behave, and how you will know it is right. A prompt asks the same of a reply or an artifact — not a different skill, a different audience. Andrew Stellman, 2025: "Prompt engineering and requirements engineering are literally the same skill — using clarity, context, and intentionality to communicate your intent."

The forms map directly. A user story — "As a [role], I want [goal], so that [benefit]" — is role plus task with a purpose clause. Given [state], When [action], Then [result] maps to context, task, and format plus checks. The ISO 29148 characteristics — unambiguous, complete, singular, verifiable — are what this chapter asks of every prompt line.

The stakes: a model guesses an unstated requirement right only about 41 percent of the time (Yang et al., 2025); a written specification deletes the guessing. Software moved first — GitHub's Spec Kit (2025) makes the written spec "the source of truth" AI agents build from, and Sean Grove of OpenAI drew the conclusion: "Whoever writes the spec... is now the programmer." One caution: this evidence is structural, measured on clarified prompts — and a model can still misinterpret a clear instruction, so verification stays necessary.

blocks.title: The hardest 80 percent, already owned
blocks.body: If you can write a procedure, a test protocol, or an acceptance criterion, you own the hardest part of prompt engineering. The elements are a requirements document in miniature.

sections.heading: Good requirements make prompts testable

blocks.text: Two ideas carry this chapter. Requirement type names what must be specified — role, context, format, method. Requirement quality describes how well any selected requirement is written. The quality bar applies the writing principles summarized by NASA (Systems Engineering Handbook, Appendix C) and INCOSE (Guide to Writing Requirements).

rows: Every line earns its place; a simple task needs a few.
Rule piles that bury what matters.
One reading; named columns, defined terms, no "etc."
Ambiguity resolved silently, the model's way.
The consequential facts and rules stated — not every fact.
The model reconciling you with yourself.
Possible with the data and tools supplied.
Confident output the data cannot support.
One requirement per line — separable, revisable.
An observable check exists: a number to reconcile, a behavior to exercise.
blocks.note: A requirement you cannot check is a wish. Separate the required outcome from a preferred implementation.

blocks.text: For a data prompt, "complete enough" means: dataset and period, row boundaries, calculation definition, deliverable, missing-data treatment, reconciliation. "Tell me which supplier is worst" leaves the model to pick the rows, the metric, and the meaning of "worst", silently; "calculate returns divided by units shipped by supplier and reconcile to the source" carries its own test.

blocks.title: Verification and validation
blocks.body: Verification: does the output meet the written criteria? Validation: does it serve the actual business need? Check both, every time — these principles improve clarity and testability without making model behavior deterministic.

sections.heading: A prompt is a small work specification

blocks.text: One worked case: a manager must choose supplier follow-up. The prompt — calculate return rate from the supplied workbook, as total returns divided by total units shipped; exclude the existing TOTAL row; return a ranked table with a brief, neutral explanation; state missing information; reconcile totals to the source. Each sentence is a requirement: audience, source, method, format, tone, check. The exclusion prevents double counting; the reconciliation makes the answer checkable. Generalized, every prompt shares one skeleton:

Purpose & audience:   help [reader] make [decision] or complete [task].
Sources & scope:      use [source / version / period]; include [scope]; exclude [items].
Selected requirements: only the types that resolve ambiguity for THIS artifact —
                      a simple task needs a few, not all.
Acceptance evidence:  check [specific result] against [source, calculation, or
                      observable test].
Missing info & boundaries: if [gap or conflict]: state it, ask, or stop.
                      Actions needing review: [actions].
blocks.caption: The skeleton of every prompt — printed on the cheat sheet (deliverables/From_Prompts_to_Agents_Cheat_Sheet.pdf).

blocks.text: The course's fuller anatomy has seven parts: five elements — Role, Task, Context, Format, Examples — plus two one-sentence safety valves, the Out and the Stop. Written out on a mundane task, the whole body is one continuous prompt of about ninety words, under two minutes to write:

ROLE      You are a precise editor. You add no facts that are not in the source.
TASK      Summarize the attached Q2 returns report for the operations lead.
CONTEXT   We're a mid-size electronics manufacturer. Return rate = returns ÷ shipped.
          The export has a totals row — exclude it.
FORMAT    ≤ 150 words: the headline number first, then three bullets.
EXAMPLES  <example> March's summary — the one the team liked </example>
THE OUT   Anything the report doesn't state: write UNKNOWN — never estimate.
          List the gaps at the end.
THE STOP  Deliver the summary, then stop — nothing beyond.
blocks.caption: Seven parts, one body. Miss a part and the prompt still works — it just fails in a predictable way, which is what makes diagnosis possible.

blocks.text: Notice the industry line: what business you are in is context — the assistant does not know your world until you say so. And note the Out's formal definition: the escape route you write for missing information — a condition, an honest move, a surfacing — so the model never has to choose between obeying you and being honest. Anthropic's golden rule applies to the whole body: show the prompt to a colleague with minimal context; if they would be confused, the model will be too.

sections.heading: Useful roles describe behavior

blocks.text: "Act as a senior analyst" is a title — a vibe the model can fake. "State your assumptions, calculate from the source, and identify what the data cannot answer" is conduct a reader can observe: either the assumptions were stated or not. The craft is decomposing an identity into personality statements — testable behaviors, not credentials — paired with a concrete question and an intended audience.

The evidence draws the boundary. Expert personas do not improve factual accuracy: 162 personas, no gain (Zheng et al., 2024), confirmed by a six-model replication (Wharton, December 2025). What a role reliably shifts is voice and register — assigned traits are identifiable in output up to 80 percent of the time (PersonaLLM, 2024). Use Role for how it answers, never instead of checking what it answers.

items: Weak: "You are a senior analyst." Strong: "You never invent numbers; you state n; you say what the data can't answer."
Weak: "You are a helpful assistant." Strong: "You challenge weak assumptions instead of agreeing; you flag uncertainty rather than smooth it over."

blocks.title: Behaviors beat titles
blocks.body: A role earns its place by naming checkable conduct, not by conferring rank — each personality statement is auditable in the output; a title is a vibe.

sections.heading: Prompt elements are requirement types: the menu

blocks.text: Role maps to behavior, context to scope, tone to communication, format to structure — and the mapping keeps going. The menu below names fourteen requirement types; you pick from it, you never fill it. Each type carries acceptance evidence — how to check compliance — in the requirements catalog, printed in full in references/Elements_of_Prompting_Field_Guide.pdf.
What the work is and who it serves

items: Functional behavior — what it must do: filter, calculate, extract, compare, explain. Weak: "analyze the returns data." Strong: "calculate the return rate per supplier and rank all three."
Scope and exclusions — in, out, explicitly outside. Weak: "use the relevant data." Strong: "detail rows only — exclude the TOTAL row; keep defects separate from returns."
Audience and use — who uses it, for which decision. Weak: "make it useful for leadership." Strong: "for a manager deciding whether supplier follow-up is warranted."
Role and working behavior — perspective plus observable conduct. Weak: "act as a reviewer." Strong: "act as a reviewer: expose assumptions and gaps."

blocks.text: What goes in and how it is computed

items: Data and provenance — allowed inputs, definitions, period, traceability. Weak: "use the supplier data." Strong: "this workbook's Data tab, 2025-09 to 2026-08 inclusive; trace each figure to its rows."

Method and business rules — formulas, denominators, missing-data treatment. Weak: "use our standard definitions." Strong: "return rate = total returns ÷ total units shipped, from sums, never averaged percentages; the 'n/a' cell is missing, not zero."
Content and completeness — required topics, fields, limitations. Weak: "cover the important points." Strong: "the business question, the comparison, one time view, a follow-up, limitations."

blocks.text: How the output looks and behaves

items: Structure and interface — sections, tabs, slides, columns, controls. Weak: "make it a nice table." Strong: "one row per supplier: Supplier | Return rate | Numerator | Denominator — highest rate first."
Tone and presentation — voice, reading level, units, number formats. Weak: "keep it short and professional." Strong: "neutral, plain language for managers; rates to three decimal places."

Accessibility and usability — labels, contrast, keyboard access, understandable language. Weak: "make it user-friendly." Strong: "labeled controls, visible focus, readable contrast, a usable narrow layout."

blocks.text: How the result is checked, bounded, and kept

items: Quality and acceptance — observable correctness criteria. Weak: "double-check your work." Strong: "reconcile total shipped and returned against the TOTAL row before presenting anything."

Constraints and authority — allowed tools, approvals, stop conditions. Weak: "be careful with the emails." Strong: "prepare the reply as a draft for review; do not send it." (Prompt instructions request compliance; actual permissions determine what a tool can do.)
Delivery and compatibility — file type, editability, offline use, destination. Weak: "send me a dashboard." Strong: "one self-contained HTML file that works offline, data embedded, no network calls."
Maintenance and reuse — refresh procedure, versions, reusable parameters. Weak: "so we can use it again." Strong: "label the file a static data snapshot with its date; keep reusable placeholders."

blocks.title: Pick, don't fill
blocks.body: The menu is a lookup aid, not a form every prompt must complete. Select the types that resolve ambiguity in this task, write each well, and define how you will check it.

sections.heading: Examples, uncertainty, and stopping

blocks.text: Examples are the strongest steering signal for format and tone: the model imitates what it sees, and on well-tuned models examples steer shape more than facts (Brown et al., 2020; Min et al., 2022). The discipline is diversity: three clones of the happy case teach only the center; one typical, one edge, and one reject case — clearly separated — teach the boundaries too. Use an edge case when it exposes a likely failure, and never smuggle obsolete facts in with the sample.

The Out is permission to not know, in checkable shape. A model is trained to always produce an answer; unless you name the honest move, inventing is the only way it can obey you. One sentence of permission cut invented answers on planted-error questions from 53 to 23 percent on GPT-4o (six-model average 66 to 44 — Omar et al., 2025), and to under 8 percent on GPT-5 (npj Digital Medicine, 2026). "Write Not stated and list the gap" is the pattern — a named form you can look for in the output.

blocks.title: Bare bans backfire
blocks.body: "Do not hallucinate" names no honest alternative, and a ban alone can trigger over-refusal of facts that are in the supplied material. Say what to do instead: the Out, plus required citations — it helps without guaranteeing that nothing is invented.

blocks.text: The Stop is the finish line: the action to perform and its boundary. Weak: "keep it focused." Strong: "answer these three questions, report limitations, then stop — do not go exploring." A completion condition converts open-ended capability into a scoped job — instead of ten charts and no answer — and in agentic work this valve grows up to become gates and autonomy rules.

blocks.title: The unifying idea
blocks.body: Each element moves something out of your head onto the page. When output disappoints, one of them stayed in your head — and the diagnosis grid below tells you which.

sections.heading: A menu of requirements for each artifact

blocks.text: The artifact decides which requirement types matter most. The working method: recognize the artifact, choose the types that resolve ambiguity in this task, then write a concrete instruction and identify the evidence that would show it was met.

items: Spreadsheet analysis — calculation rules: row grain, period, metric definitions, denominators, missing values, reconciliation.
Interactive dashboards — behavior and state: date ranges, filters, coordinated views, empty and zero states, Reset, offline portability.
Presentations — narrative and editability: audience, story structure, one message per slide, data fidelity, speaker notes.
Email briefs — chronology and evidence: current versus superseded positions, decisions with conditions, owners and dates, the draft-only boundary.
Plain-language documents — reading level and fidelity: vocabulary, structure, analogy limits, preserved conditions, a comprehension check.

blocks.text: The per-artifact tables — requirement type, example instruction, how to check it — are printed in the field guide; the same menus drive the Prompt Template Creator (deliverables/Prompt_Template_Creator.html) and the Configurator (references/Prompt_Template_Configurator.xlsx). Treat it as a catalog: something disappointed, name the weak spot, pick a stronger fill. You do not study it; you look things up in it.

sections.heading: The improvement loop

blocks.text: A first prompt is a draft, and the way from draft to dependable is a loop you may already run on processes: Plan, Do, Check, Act — the improvement cycle of W. Edwards Deming, which Toyota built its production system around. The Lean Enterprise Institute published a piece in May 2026 applying it to prompting as "Prompt, Do, Check, Act"; their observation: the people who get the most from these tools are the ones willing to run the loop a few more times. Every phase can be partly delegated while judgment stays with you.

items: Plan — draft the ask. Fill the elements the task needs; say why behind each rule; separate instructions from pasted material; show examples, one edge case included. Delegate it: "I need [X] for [audience], with [constraints]. Draft me a strong prompt, then wait."
Do — run it, in order. Number the steps; add "wait for my OK" where you want control; documents on top, ask at the end; fresh chat per topic.

Check — inspect before you trust. Name the failed element with the grid below; self-check against named criteria — never "are you sure?"; blind-review by pasting the draft as "a colleague's"; reconcile numbers to a total you already trust.

Act — refine, then standardize. Fix one element and rerun the affected check — never reword at random; when a prompt passes representative checks, name it, version it, save it; re-baseline on every model upgrade. Delegate it: "Rewrite this prompt so it more consistently produces X."

rows: the wrong altitude, tone, or posture
an answer to a different (or vaguer) question
generically right, specifically wrong for us
right content, unusable shape or length
not matching the standard in your head
blocks.note: The symptom-to-element diagnosis grid — also in the EX-Report tab of deliverables/Course_Workbook.xlsx. Name the failed element, fix that one, rerun.

blocks.text: Keep a change only when it improves the result on representative examples, not one lucky run. Model self-review helps find issues, but it is not proof — the checks that count compare the output with evidence or a known calculation.

sections.heading: One task through the improvement loop

blocks.text: The loop at its smallest, on the supplier case. Initial ask: "Summarize supplier returns." Observed problem: the total includes a pre-calculated TOTAL row — units counted twice. Revision, aimed at that failure: "Use detail rows only; exclude the TOTAL row." Verification: compare with the source total — an independent check only when scope, filters, and units match. Change the instruction linked to the failure; keep the business question stable. A passing test supports reuse; it does not establish universal reliability.
Run enough turns and the one-line ask grows into the full analysis prompt — each added line a requirement type fixing one named weakness:

Use Course_Workbook.xlsx, Data tab, detail rows only — exclude the TOTAL row (144 rows; one Inspection_Hours cell is "n/a": treat it as missing, not zero, and disclose it). One row = one month × site × supplier; period 2025-09 to 2026-08 inclusive. Question: which supplier has the highest RETURN RATE, defined as total Units_Returned ÷ total Units_Shipped per supplier over the full period — computed from sums, never by averaging monthly percentages. Keep Defects_Found separate from returns; do not add them together. Rank the three suppliers showing numerator and denominator, reconcile total shipped and returned against the TOTAL row, and state one limitation of the comparison. Then stop.
blocks.caption: The staged build-up with commentary is tab 1-Analyze-Data of deliverables/Course_Workbook.xlsx.

blocks.title: Expected output for the supplier case
blocks.body: 144 detail rows; 224,902 units shipped, 432 returns, reconciling to the TOTAL row; defects (2,207) separate. Highest return rate: Bravo Plastics 0.348% (262 ÷ 75,184), then Cardinal Metals 0.129% (96 ÷ 74,658), Alpha Components 0.099% (74 ÷ 75,060).

blocks.text: One clarification: the anatomy is the design layer — what a prompt contains; is it complete? The loop is the process layer — what you do with it; how does it get, and stay, good? In chat you run the loop by hand between turns; in agentic work you write the loop into the brief itself, which is why it works best there:

PLAN   Role: careful retail analyst — never invent numbers. Task: monthly returns
       report from the attached export. Context: columns = SKU · reason code ·
       refund €. Format: one-page summary + top-5 table. Example: last month's
       report, attached. The out: field missing → say so, don't guess.
       The stop: deliver the report — nothing beyond.
DO     1) Read the export; list the columns you actually see. 2) WAIT for my OK.
       3) Build the table. 4) Draft the summary.
CHECK  Before showing me anything: reconcile the table to the export TOTAL.
       If it doesn't reconcile, STOP and report the gap.
ACT    Deliver the final report. Then list what was ambiguous in this brief,
       so I can fix it for next month.
blocks.caption: The loop written into one brief: a wait-gate is a Do you kept; a stop-on-fail Check is a verification you refused to delegate.

blocks.title: Two layers, one craft
blocks.body: You write with the anatomy; you improve with the loop. And Act does both of its jobs: deliver the output, and name what to improve — the prompt asks for its own next revision.

sections.heading: Prompt techniques to test

blocks.text: Treat every technique as a hypothesis to test on representative examples: research effects depend on the model, task, data, and measurement, and one benchmark is not a universal effect size. Still, the evidence sorts advice into three piles.

blocks.title: Replicated — reliably helps
blocks.body: Specificity, grounding, structure, and named checks survive replication across models — the elements of this chapter, measured.

items: Be specific — task, constraints, success criteria: unstated needs are guessed right only about 41 percent of the time.
One tested, reused template with delimiters: formatting alone can swing accuracy up to 76 points (Sclar et al., 2024).
Long inputs: documents on top, question at the end — worth up to roughly 30 percent.
An out in checkable shape, plus required citations: invented answers cut by a third or more.
Self-check against named criteria: fact scores jumped 56 to 71 with planned verification (Chain-of-Verification, 2024).
Ask the assistant to improve your prompt: optimizer-written prompts beat human ones; every major vendor ships an official improver.

blocks.title: Never survived replication
blocks.body: Flattery, threats, and magic phrases move style at best and add noise at worst. "The AI knows what I mean" is the same 41 percent from the other side — say what you mean is the cure.

items: Expert personas for accuracy: zero gain across 162 personas.
Tips, threats, "important to my career": null on average; the famous gain was a cherry-picked best case.
Magic phrases ("take a deep breath"): each won on one model, one benchmark — never universally.
"Longer prompts are better": padding drops reasoning accuracy at around 3,000 filler tokens — density wins.
"Are you sure?" as verification: answers flip under pushback in 58 percent of cases (SycEval, 2025).

blocks.title: Was right — then the product absorbed it
blocks.body: "Think step by step" was real — one math benchmark went from 10 to 41 percent in 2022 — until vendors built the stepping into reasoning models. Advice expires when the product absorbs it.

items: Manual chain-of-thought: pick a reasoning model and set the effort level (still legitimate on small local models).
Piles of examples: start zero-shot; add three to five format-definers only when shape drifts.
"You are a world-class expert" for accuracy: persona for voice only.
Carrying an old prompt stack onto each model: re-baseline on every upgrade — strip to the anatomy, re-test, re-add what earns its place.

blocks.text: The full lists, with the study behind every line, are in the PLAYBOOK tab of deliverables/Course_Workbook.xlsx; the field guide's evidence compendium carries the why per verdict. What holds throughout: clarity, context, format, the Out, grounding, iteration — scaffolding tricks retire; briefing skills compound.

sections.heading: A neutral rubric reduces leading feedback

blocks.text: One bias corrupts the Check phase specifically. AI mirrors you: across eleven leading models, AI affirmed the user about half again as often as a person would — plus 49 percent (Stanford and Carnegie Mellon, in Science, 2026). The cause is structural: models are trained on human preference data, and humans prefer agreement. The pattern made headlines first: in April 2025 OpenAI rolled back a ChatGPT update it called, in its own words, "overly flattering or agreeable... sycophantic"; in June 2025 the New York Times reported chatbots validating false beliefs; in August 2025 Microsoft's AI chief warned of unhealthy AI validation.

The countermeasure is in how you ask. A leading request — "I think this is excellent. Tell me why it works" — embeds the preferred conclusion in the task. A neutral one names a rubric and invites disconfirmation: "Evaluate this against clarity, evidence, and completeness. Identify weaknesses and what would change your assessment." Compare reasoning and evidence — a harsher answer is not automatically more accurate either. Never reveal your preferred answer; ask for the case against; paste your own draft as a colleague's; treat agreement under pushback as noise.

blocks.title: See the mirror yourself
blocks.body: Two chats, same paragraph. One: "A colleague wrote this — rate it 1-10, three biggest weaknesses." Two: "I wrote this myself and I'm really proud of it — rate it 1-10, three biggest weaknesses." Did the score move once it knew you were the author?

blocks.text: With the bias named, the chapter compresses into a review checklist. Clarity: one identifiable task, explicit definitions, a useful output. Relevance: only instructions and source material that help the task. Boundaries: missing-information behavior, a completion condition, authority limits where actions are involved. Evidence: a source check, a calculation check, or an observable acceptance test. Test advice in your actual workflow — more words, stronger praise, or a magic phrase cannot guarantee a better result.

sections.heading: Optional practice: a course-log study aid

blocks.text: If you have been running this book's exercises in one chat — the course log the workbook's first exercise sets up — close the chapter by turning that log into a study aid:

Using the course notes and prompts in this conversation, create a study aid.

List the concepts, one useful example of each, the checks I used, and two
questions I still need to resolve.

Separate what I demonstrated from what I only read about.
blocks.caption: Run it in the course-log chat. A two-step variant — list every prompt run, then build a one-page report — is in the EX-Report tab of deliverables/Course_Workbook.xlsx.

blocks.text: Notice the craft inside the request: it names the content requirements, and the last line is an honesty boundary. The workbook version carries an Out ("anything the log doesn't show: write UNKNOWN — don't invent") and a Stop ("deliver the report, then stop") — the course's own rules applied to the course. The result doubles as the first entry in your prompt library: name it, date it, keep it. If the log was lost, the numbered prompts in the workbook tabs are the full list — rebuild from there.

blocks.title: What a generated summary proves
blocks.body: Generated reflection supports recall; it does not prove skill. The demonstration that you can do the work is the capstone task, checked against its own acceptance evidence.

title: Putting prompts to work: one case, five artifacts
intro: Everything so far has been about writing requirements. This part puts them to work on a single running case: a fictional supplier-quality question that travels through five artifacts - a data analysis, an interactive dashboard, a management presentation, an email brief, and a plain-language explanation. The data, the prompts, and the checked answers all ship with the course, so you can run every step yourself and verify every number you produce.

sections.heading: One question, five artifacts

blocks.text: The question is deliberately ordinary: which supplier has the highest return rate, and what should we investigate next? A manufacturer receives components from three fictional suppliers - Alpha Components, Bravo Plastics, and Cardinal Metals - at four sites (Austin, Berlin, Osaka, Monterrey), and the practice workbook records twelve months of deliveries, September 2025 through August 2026. All names and numbers are generated for training; nothing in the case is real company data, so you can upload it wherever your policies allow.

That one question runs through five artifacts in order: analyze the data, explore it in an interactive dashboard, present the findings, extract decisions from an email thread, and explain a topic clearly. The first three share the same cleaned records and the same verified numbers; the last two change the input but keep the discipline. Everything lives in Course_Workbook.xlsx: tabs 1-Analyze-Data through 5-Explain-Clearly carry the five tasks in order, the Data tab holds the raw records, and Data_Clean holds the checked detail set the later tasks use. Prepared outputs sit in references/exercise-data/, so every exercise has a checked fallback.

Why one case instead of five? Because the requirement types recur, and the artifact decides which ones matter: calculation rules for a spreadsheet analysis, behavior and state for a dashboard, narrative and editability for a presentation, chronology and evidence for an email brief, reading level and fidelity for a plain-language document. Watching the same facts pass through five shapes makes that pattern visible.
A basic prompt, and what it decides for you
Analyze the supplier data and tell me which supplier is worst.
blocks.caption: The starter prompt - workbook tab 1-Analyze-Data. Run it once before improving it.

blocks.text: This prompt runs, and it returns something confident. But it made three decisions silently: which rows to use, which metric to compute, and what "worst" means. Spelled out, the gaps are: no source scope, no metric definition, no denominator rule, no missing-data rule, and no check. Every gap becomes the model's guess - and a guess you cannot see is a guess you cannot audit.
The improved prompt

Use Course_Workbook.xlsx, Data tab, detail rows only — exclude the TOTAL row (144 rows; one Inspection_Hours cell is "n/a": treat it as missing, not zero, and disclose it). One row = one month × site × supplier; period 2025-09 to 2026-08 inclusive. Question: which supplier has the highest RETURN RATE, defined as total Units_Returned ÷ total Units_Shipped per supplier over the full period — computed from sums, never by averaging monthly percentages. Keep Defects_Found separate from returns; do not add them together. Rank the three suppliers showing numerator and denominator, reconcile total shipped and returned against the TOTAL row, and state one limitation of the comparison. Then stop.
blocks.caption: The improved analysis prompt, verbatim - workbook tab 1-Analyze-Data.

blocks.text: Read it line by line and every addition maps to a requirement type from the elements lesson. The catalog in references/Requirements_by_Artifact.md carries the full menu for spreadsheet analysis - row grain, reporting period, field types and units, duplicates and summary rows, metric definition, weighting and denominators, missing values, segmentation, verification and limitations, delivery - each paired with the acceptance evidence that proves it was met.

rows: Names the file, the Data tab, detail rows only
Return rate = total returns / total shipped, from sums
"n/a" is missing, not zero, and disclosed
Reconcile to TOTAL row; one limitation; then stop

blocks.title: Write the requirement, not the wish
blocks.body: A prompt improves by adding the requirement that fixes a specific observed weakness. Each added line names one gap and closes it; nothing is added for decoration.

sections.heading: Task 1: analyze spreadsheet data

blocks.text: Open the Data tab of Course_Workbook.xlsx. One row is one month-site-supplier observation. Units_Shipped counts units received that month; Units_Returned counts units customers later returned for component defects - the escapes; Defects_Found counts defective units caught at incoming inspection. Keeping those last two apart is the case's first discipline. Inspection_Hours, Unit_Cost_USD, and On_Time_Percent complete the row; On_Time_Percent is a monthly percentage, a detail that matters later. The workbook's README tab defines every column - a ready-made data block you can paste into a prompt rather than retype.

Two quirks are planted on purpose, and both are documented in that README tab: the last row of the Data tab is a TOTAL row that must be excluded from any calculation, and one Inspection_Hours cell contains the text "n/a". A good first prompt finds both - which is exactly why the task starts with a profile, not a question.

blocks.title: Profile first, analyze second
blocks.body: Inspect the data and its boundaries before asking for conclusions. Make the model look at the file and report what it sees; only then ask your question.

blocks.text: Inspect before you calculate

Inspect the Data tab before calculating.

Report the detail-row count, column meanings, missing values, and any summary rows that could be counted twice.

Explain what you would include or exclude, then wait.
blocks.caption: The inspection exercise. "Then wait" is the working boundary: no analysis until the profile is confirmed.

blocks.title: Success check
blocks.body: A good profile reports 144 detail rows, one TOTAL row to exclude, and one missing inspection-hours value. If it missed a quirk, tell it and make it re-profile - that correction is what the step is for.

blocks.text: The two quirks need different treatment. The TOTAL row is redundant information: including it double counts every value, so it is excluded - but kept nearby, because it becomes the reconciliation anchor in a moment. The "n/a" cell is absent information: it must stay missing, never become zero, and any calculation that excludes it must say so. Exclusion and disclosure are different obligations.
Compare suppliers and check the result

Using detail rows only, calculate return rate by supplier:

total Units_Returned ÷ total Units_Shipped.

Rank suppliers from highest to lowest. Reconcile the shipped and returned totals. Explain one limitation of the comparison.
blocks.caption: The comparison exercise - the compact core of the improved prompt.

blocks.text: Whether you run this compact version or the full improved prompt, the result is checkable to the digit:

blocks.note: Defects found - 2,207 occurrences caught at incoming inspection - are a separate measure. Their sum with returns is not a count of distinct defective units.

blocks.text: Bravo Plastics has the highest return rate, roughly three and a half times Alpha's, and the shipped and returned sums reconcile exactly against the TOTAL row. A defensible limitation to state: the data show which supplier has more returns, not why - nothing in these columns establishes a cause.

blocks.title: Confidence is not the deliverable
blocks.body: Correct calculations, honest limits, and reconciliation matter more than confident prose. A ranked table with numerator, denominator, one reconciliation, and one stated limitation is a complete answer.

blocks.text: Extend the analysis

STEP 2 · TREND — For the highest-return supplier: monthly return rate (that month's returns ÷ that month's shipments) for 2025-09 to 2026-08, as a table. Is it improving, worsening, or volatile? Describe the pattern only — do not claim a cause.

STEP 3 · SITES — Return rate by site (same definition, same period), ranked. Do particular sites drive the supplier difference? Compare only on equal scope.

STEP 4 · DENOMINATORS — Can this data support an overall on-time delivery rate? Explain using only the columns available, and name the extra data that would be needed.

TRANSFER — Rewrite the improved prompt for a dataset from your own work: keep every requirement type, change only the specifics.
blocks.caption: Follow-up prompts, verbatim - workbook tab 1-Analyze-Data.

blocks.text: The trend question has a checkable answer too: Bravo's monthly return rate is elevated and volatile rather than steadily worsening - it peaks near 0.737% in April 2026, drops to roughly 0.14% in the quiet months of June and July 2026, and sits near 0.465% in August 2026. Accept "volatile, no steady improvement"; reject any answer that names a cause.

The on-time question is the denominator lesson in miniature, and the expected answer is no. On_Time_Percent is a monthly percentage with no delivery counts behind it, so no overall on-time delivery rate can be computed from this file. The honest move is to label any average as an unweighted mean of monthly percentages - Alpha 91.7646, Bravo 92.5333, Cardinal 92.0833 - state plainly that these are not overall delivery rates, and name the missing data a true rate would need: delivery counts per month.

One reference finding sharpens the follow-up question the case builds toward. Units-weighted unit costs are $12.4299 for Alpha, $9.9030 for Bravo, and $14.1804 for Cardinal: the cheapest supplier also has the highest return rate, and the data cannot say why. Any follow-up you propose in the later artifacts has to carry that tension honestly. Save the verified analysis - the dashboard and the presentation reuse it.
Common wrong turns

blocks.title: Five ways to be confidently wrong
blocks.body: Each of these produces a plausible-looking answer. The improved prompt forbids all five explicitly, and the acceptance checks below catch them when it fails to.

items: Averaging the monthly return-rate percentages instead of dividing summed returns by summed shipments - months with different volumes get equal weight, so the denominator is wrong.

Adding Defects_Found to Units_Returned and calling the sum "defective units" - inspection catches and customer returns are different measures, and their sum is not a count of distinct defective units.
Treating the "n/a" Inspection_Hours cell as zero - a missing measurement is not a measurement of nothing.
Including the TOTAL row, which double counts every column it summarizes.
Explaining the result - "Bravo's process causes the returns" - when the data supports association at most, never a cause.

blocks.text: Acceptance checks

items: Row count: exactly 144 detail rows in scope after excluding the TOTAL row.
Reconciliation: summed shipments and returns match the TOTAL row exactly - 224,902 units and 432 returns.
Traceability: the displayed 0.348% recomputes from its parts, 262 returns over 75,184 units.
Disclosure: the missing Inspection_Hours value is named wherever it affects a calculation.
Limits: one limitation is stated, and comparative language stays at association, not cause.

blocks.text: The full worked key ships in the workbook's KEY-Analysis tab (instructor material) and in the course deck's reference appendix, so a self-study reader can grade their own run without a facilitator in the room.

sections.heading: Task 2: build a dashboard you can check

blocks.text: The second artifact changes the deliverable from an answer to a tool. The input is references/exercise-data/Supplier_Data_Clean.csv - the same 144 checked detail rows the analysis validated, one per month, site, and supplier, with the missing inspection-hours value left blank rather than zeroed. The output is one self-contained HTML file that opens from disk, offline, with the data embedded and every number computed from the embedded records.

blocks.title: You specify behavior, not code
blocks.body: The page provides the structure; JavaScript supplies the interactive behavior. You specify a dashboard's behavior in plain language, control by control - no code knowledge is needed to ask for it precisely.

blocks.text: Workbook tab 2-Build-Dashboard stages the build the way the improvement loop taught: a core prompt that produces the artifact, a behavior pass that adds the controls, a states pass that pins down empty, missing, and zero, and then a check with a known answer. The optional EX-Dashboard tab adds one more discipline in front: a shape stage, in which the assistant proposes the KPIs, their formulas, targets, and the layout as plain text and stops before writing any code. A wrong KPI caught at that gate costs a sentence; caught after the dashboard circulates, it costs a retraction. The rhythm is shape, build, check, refine - and refine means one named change at a time, re-verifying any number the change touched.

From the attached data file, build ONE self-contained HTML file that works offline from disk. Views: summary tiles, one chart, and a sortable table of the records — data embedded, every number computed from the embedded records, metric definitions and the snapshot date in the footer. Controls, wired so one selection re-scopes every view: a month-range selector with inclusive endpoints · category multi-select filters · a comparison switch · a monthly/quarterly granularity switch · a metric selector · drill-down from a chart segment to its underlying records · ranking on the selected measure · Reset. Show active selections; an empty selection says "no matching records"; missing values stay blank; a zero denominator shows "—". Label the file a static data snapshot with its date.
blocks.caption: The complete dashboard prompt, verbatim. Tab 2-Build-Dashboard carries the same content staged as prompts you run in sequence.

blocks.text: What makes a KPI worth a tile
A KPI is a number someone acts on, not decoration. Before you approve a tile row, hold each candidate against four tests:

items: A decision. If nobody would do anything differently when the number moves, it is trivia, not a KPI - cut it.
A formula. Named columns and exact arithmetic; if you cannot write the formula, you cannot track the number.
A target. A value is a fact; value-versus-target is a status.
Three views. Every KPI answers level (where are we), trend (which way is it moving), and gap (how far from target). Tiles show level and gap; the chart shows trend.

blocks.text: Name the parts and you can ask for them

Each control earns its place by answering a business question: the month range and the granularity switch answer when did it change?; the supplier and site filters and the comparison switch answer who is different?; the metric selector answers different on what?; drill-down answers which records back this number?; and Reset makes exploration safe. Controls are questions, not decoration - add one only when its question matters. A few vocabulary essentials carry most requests:

rows: Big-number card: value, vs-target state, trend arrow
"A KPI row of four tiles across the top."
Change vs the prior period, beside the value
"Each tile shows the delta vs last month."
Tiny axis-less trend line inside a tile
Bar chart sorted by value - who is worst
"Ranked bars of return rate by site, worst first."
Grid colored by value, two dimensions at once
One control that narrows every view at once
"Site and Supplier filters that apply to all views."
From a chart segment to its underlying rows
"Click a segment to show its records."
When the data was last refreshed, on the page
"Footer: as-of date, source, owner, refresh cadence."
blocks.note: The full twenty-term vocabulary with ready-made phrasings is in the workbook's EX-Dashboard tab. It is the transferable part - the same words work in Power BI and Tableau conversations.

blocks.text: Empty, missing, and zero are three different facts
Show the active selections at all times. An empty selection must say "no matching records" — distinguish it from a real zero. Missing values stay blank; a zero denominator shows "—", never an error.
blocks.caption: The states pass, verbatim - workbook tab 2-Build-Dashboard.

blocks.text: An empty selection means no records matched; a zero means records matched and the value really is zero; a blank means the value was never measured. A dashboard that collapses these into one symbol will eventually be read wrong in exactly the meeting where it matters. The zero-denominator dash prevents the ugliest failure of all: a division error styled as a number.
The check that makes it trustworthy

Filter to Site = Berlin, Supplier = Bravo Plastics, months 2026-03 to 2026-08. Expect exactly 6 records, 8,575 units shipped, 21 returns, return rate 0.245% — in the tiles, the chart, AND the table. Verify independently by filtering the Data tab the same way.
blocks.caption: The acceptance check, verbatim - workbook tab 2-Build-Dashboard.

blocks.title: The filtered check
blocks.body: Berlin and Bravo Plastics, March through August 2026: exactly 6 records, 8,575 units shipped, 21 returns, 0.245% return rate - in the tiles, the chart, and the table at once, with rates recomputed from the filtered sums.

blocks.text: This is the coordinated-views requirement made concrete: one selection re-scopes every view, so the tiles, the chart, and the table can never disagree about which records are on screen. One verified filtered result beats any amount of admiring the design. The fuller dashboard menu - input contract, date range, category controls, filter combination, coordinated views, empty and zero states, reset, accessibility, portability, performance - is in references/Requirements_by_Artifact.md, each type with its acceptance evidence.
The prepared fallback, and two cautions

A finished, checked build ships in the package: references/exercise-data/Supplier_Quality_Dashboard.html, built from the same cleaned records and metric definitions as your analysis. Open it offline, run the Berlin filter yourself, and read the footer: it carries the definitions, the snapshot date, and a self-check that runs this same filtered comparison - it must say PASSED. If your own build stalls, the fallback lets you study working behavior first and rebuild later.

Building the file yourself needs an assistant that writes and packages code into a downloadable HTML file. As of September 2026 that means Claude (Artifacts), ChatGPT (Canvas), or Gemini (Canvas), typically on paid tiers; in Copilot it means Pages, not plain chat. If your tool only chats, the specification still has value - hand it to IT as written, or ask for an Excel version of the same views.

blocks.title: A snapshot, not a system
blocks.body: The file embeds its data, so classify and share it like the spreadsheet it came from - share the file, not a public link. And label it what it is: a static data snapshot with its date, not a live reporting system. Refreshing data is a job for a BI tool.

sections.heading: Task 3: present the findings

blocks.text: The supplier case now changes audience. Your verified analysis answered the analyst's question - Bravo Plastics has the highest return rate, 262 returns against 75,184 units shipped, 0.348% - but a management audience does not want to see the analyst's screen. It wants a decision framed, evidence it can trust, and a visible boundary between what the data show and what you propose to do about it. A presentation is a deliverable with its own artifact requirements, and writing the prompt means choosing them deliberately.

For a management deck, eight requirement types carry the weight: purpose and audience (name the decision and the intended action), scope and slide count (five slides with a defined coverage list), story structure (from business question to evidence, implications, and next action), message hierarchy (one main message per slide), data fidelity (only checked findings, with period, units, and limitations preserved), chart semantics (truthful axes, labeled categories), speaker notes, and editability and delivery (an editable .pptx you can actually present). The full menu, with an acceptance check for each type, is the presentations table in references/Requirements_by_Artifact.md.

Create an editable five-slide management presentation using only the verified analysis. The audience must decide what follow-up is warranted. Cover: the business question and scope · the comparison · one useful time or segment view · a proposed follow-up · limitations with next steps. Give each slide one main message, readable evidence, accurate units and reporting period, and brief speaker notes. Preserve uncertainty and missing-data limits. Do not invent causes or unsupported benefits. Check every number against the analysis and inspect the exported slides for clipping and readability.
blocks.caption: The reusable presentation prompt - copy-paste cell in workbook tab 3-Present-Findings.

blocks.text: The mock deck, slide by slide

The prepared output this prompt produced is Supplier_Quality_Mock_Presentation.pptx in references/exercise-data/ - a fictional five-slide management deck built only from the verified analysis, in a deliberately distinct navy look so it never reads as part of the course deck. Open it beside Course_Workbook.xlsx; every number on it traces to the workbook.

items: Question and scope - one question (which supplier has the highest return rate, and what should we investigate next?), one period (2025-09 to 2026-08), four receiving sites, three suppliers, 144 delivery records, one definition: return rate is total units returned divided by total units shipped, the same scope for every comparison. The decision the deck supports is named on the title slide: is a supplier follow-up warranted?

The comparison - a bar chart with the numbers beside it: Bravo Plastics 262 returns / 75,184 shipped = 0.348%; Cardinal Metals 96 / 74,658 = 0.129%; Alpha Components 74 / 75,060 = 0.099%. A side note closes the obvious objection: shipment volumes are nearly equal, so the rate gap is not a volume artifact.

The trend - Bravo's monthly return rate across the twelve months: elevated and volatile, peaking at 0.737% in April 2026, quiet near 0.14% in June and July, back at 0.465% in August. The commentary says only what twelve points can support: no steady improvement - and no claim of seasonality or cause.

The proposed follow-up - a two-panel slide. Left, labeled findings: the rate gap, its persistence, and the separate fact that Bravo drives 1,157 of the 2,207 inspection defect occurrences. Right, labeled judgment: ask Bravo for a returns root-cause review, pull the records behind the highest-return months, agree a target and re-measure next quarter on the same definition.

Limitations and next steps - descriptive, not causal; no delivery counts exist, so no overall delivery rate is claimed anywhere; one inspection-hours value is missing (missing, not zero); inspection defects and customer returns are two measures that are never added together. Then the single decision requested: approve the review.

blocks.text: The separation rule

Findings are what the workbook supports; recommendations are labeled proposals. The mock deck makes the boundary physical - two panels, two headings - because that separation is the trust move that survives every audience question. It matters most exactly where the story gets tempting. The verified scorecard carries units-weighted unit costs: Alpha Components $12.4299, Bravo Plastics $9.9030, Cardinal Metals $14.1804. The tension is real - the cheapest supplier is also the most-returned - and it is precisely where a weak deck starts inventing: a projected savings figure, a quality-cost trade-off, a committed benefit. The mock deck states no cost claim anywhere, because the data cannot support one; what switching or fixing would cost is a question for the proposed review, not for this dataset.

blocks.title: The invented benefit
blocks.body: The prompt forbids invented causes and unsupported benefits for a reason: a decision audience remembers the number you made up, not the caveat you attached to it. Bravo's low unit cost ($9.9030 against $12.4299 and $14.1804) invites a savings story the workbook cannot back - leave it out.

blocks.text: Check it like an artifact

items: Coverage: count five slides and map each one to the coverage list in the prompt.
Fidelity: reconcile every displayed number to the analysis - at minimum trace the 0.348% comparison and the April 2026 peak of 0.737% back to the workbook.
Narrative: read only the slide titles. Do they tell the story alone, from question to evidence to proposal to limits?
Delivery: open the exported file and inspect it - no clipped text, readable at projection size, speaker notes present on every slide, charts still editable.

blocks.title: Not decorated bullet points
blocks.body: A presentation is an artifact with narrative, fidelity, and delivery requirements. One main message per slide, every number traced to the source, and the limitations named out loud are what let the deck survive its first hard question.

blocks.title: Audit before reuse
blocks.body: Run the four checks on Supplier_Quality_Mock_Presentation.pptx before you reuse the prompt on your own analysis. The sample is deliberately auditable - the limitations slide names what the data cannot say, which is the habit to copy.
